This is game 13 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll stay at 20k for game 13, focus on securing eye space and counting area early, and save the full game plus a concrete review for the next session.

# Game 11: Black vs 20k — B+2

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 58–59: 59 total moves, 56 stone moves and three passes (56, 58, 59).
Final captures: Black 1, White 0. No invalid move, ko, resignation or dead-stone removal occurred.

This is the first Black win and second consecutive win at 20k, following five losses there. Retain 20k to establish repeatability; neither the opening nor the corner rescue is proven best or forced.

## Records and verified score

- game-011.sgf contains all 59 moves.
- game-011-log.json contains opponent selection, all 30 play responses, every returned board, current-board group/liberty and empty-region inventories, full move list, in-game counting notes and verified final area.
- Official result: Black wins by 2 points.
- Independent count: Black 29 stones + 16 territory = 45; White 26 stones + 10 territory = 36. White plus komi = 43. All 81 points assigned, no neutral area.
- Lower Black region: 19 stones + 14 empty points = 33.
- Upper-right Black region: nine connected stones + isolated J9 + two separate eyes = 12.
- Lower region by rows: row 1 all nine; row 2 all nine; row 3 A/B/C/F/G/H (six); row 4 A/B/C/G (four); row 5 A/B/C/D (four); row 6 B6 (one). Total 33.
- Upper region by rows: row 6 H6 (one); row 7 F/G/H/J (four); row 8 F/G/H/J (four); row 9 G/H/J (three). Total 12.
- Black territory: A1/A2/A3/A4/B1/B2/B3/B4/C1/D1/E1/F1, G2, J1, H9, J8.
- White territory: A8/A9/B8/B9/C8/C9/D7/D8/D9, F5.

## Opening and connections

1 B C3, 2 W E5, 3 B G7, 4 W C7,
5 B G3, 6 W E3, 7 B C5, 8 W G5,
9 B E2, 10 W F4, 11 B F3, 12 W H4,
13 B H3, 14 W J3, 15 B J2, 16 W J4,
17 B H2, 18 W E7, 19 B F2, 20 W D3,
21 B D2, 22 W D4, 23 B C4, 24 W C6,
25 B D5, 26 W E4, 27 B G4, 28 W H5,
29 B C2, 30 W F6.

E2 contested the lower side beneath White E3. F3 connected to G3; H3 blocked the right-side descent. J2 put J3 in atari, White J4 connected it to H4, and Black H2 promptly connected J2 to the lower chain. F2 joined E2 to F3. D2 and C2 later connected the entire lower and left framework; C4 had already joined C3 to C5.

D5 put White D3/D4/E3 in atari; White E4 joined those stones to E5 and F4. Black G4 occupied a central boundary point, but White H5 joined its right stones. White's E6/F5 connections remained available. Present low liberties were pressure, not a demonstrated capture: both E6 and F5 were surrounded by White and were unplayable for Black without a capture.

After move 10, an explicitly unsecured row outline gave 48 possible Black points: rows 1/2 nine each, row 3 eight excluding E3, row 4 ABC/GHJ six, row 5 ABC/HJ five, row 6 HJ two, and rows 7/8/9 GHJ three each. None was secure territory. This was a useful warning about the small margin, but a coarse geometric outline, not a validated territorial estimate. In particular the right-middle region was reduced substantially.

## Upper fight: preserve connections, then recognize the actual eye shape

31 B F7, 32 W D6, 33 B F8, 34 W E8,
35 B H6, 36 W F9, 37 B G9, 38 W E9,
39 B G8, 40 W G6, 41 B H7, 42 W J8,
43 B J7, 44 W J5, 45 B J9, 46 W E6,
47 B H8 captured White J8, 48 W J6.

F7/F8 developed the upper base. H6 still needed connection. G9 put White F9 in atari; after White E9 connected it, G8 immediately joined G9 to F8/G7. H7 then joined H6 to the upper group after White G6 closed the center. These connections preserved every Black stone.

The eye space was dangerously narrow when White invaded J8. J7 contained its downward route. J9 at move 45 had only H9 and was deliberately played in atari. It reduced White J8 to H8, but White could capture J9 by H9 at that moment. Actual White E6 instead connected the central groups and ignored both ataris.

Black H8 then captured J8. Crucially, that capture opened J8 as a second liberty for isolated Black J9: J9 now had H9 AND J8. White J6 removed the main group's outside liberty, but the two eye points remained.

Exact final life proof:
- Main upper group: F7/F8/G7/G8/G9/H6/H7/H8/J7, liberties exactly H9 and J8.
- Isolated J9: liberties exactly H9 and J8.
- H9 is a separate one-point empty region bordered by G9/H8/J9, all Black.
- J8 is a separate one-point empty region bordered by H8/J7/J9, all Black.
- White H9 would leave BOTH Black groups their J8 liberty, capture neither, and have zero liberties itself: suicide.
- White J8 likewise leaves both groups H9 and is suicide.

This is unconditional life for two Black groups sharing two fully enclosed eyes. The boundaries are not all one connected chain, but each boundary group retains the other eye. This differs from game 6's opposing-color shared liberties and from game 9's one-liberty A1 boundary that could be captured into ko. Do NOT fill H9 or J8 to connect J9: doing so leaves the joined group only the other eye and allows its capture.

The successful J9/H8 continuation depended on White E6 at move 46. It is not a forced rescue. A manually considered alternative W H9 captures J9, followed by B H8 capturing three, would produce bent-three H9/J9/J8; Black would still need the dividing J9 move, while White moves first. Do not call that alternative alive. Earlier upper eye-space preservation remains a task; no single replacement is verified.

## Area-driven left expansion and lower life

After move 48, the upper region was safely 12. The lower outline was 32: together only 44, insufficient for a Black win. This concrete count changed the plan.

49 B B6, 50 W B7, 51 B B5 connected B6,
52 W A6, 53 B A5, 54 W A7.

B6 added one point outside the earlier lower outline. B5 repaired its two-liberty connection immediately; A5 blocked White's undercut and put A6 in atari, so White A7 connected to B7. The actual lower region then contained 33 points, giving Black 45 overall. This demonstrates the played gain, not that B6 forces it against every reply.

55 B H1, 56 W pass, 57 B G1, 58 W pass, 59 B pass.

H1 joined H2 and made J1 a true eye (H1/J2 boundaries).
G1 joined through H1 and made G2 a separate true eye (F2/G3/H2/G1 boundaries).
All those boundary stones belong to the connected lower group. The twelve-point left/bottom space was additional territory; lower life did not depend on resisting an invasion there. Black did not immediately pass after White's first pass: G1 completed the explicit two-eye proof before accepting the B+2 count.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k. There are now two wins, one with each color, after five losses at that rank. Repeatability is improving but remains a small sample.
2. Make area counting drive an action. Upper 12 plus lower 32 was only 44; B6/B5/A5 produced the extra point in this actual game. Count secured regions separately from early outlines.
3. Repair the new stone's connection promptly: J2–H2, E2–F2, G9–G8, H6–H7 and B6–B5 all survived.
4. Rebuild liberties after a capture. H8 removed J8 and gave isolated J9 its second liberty, changing the life proof.
5. Connected boundaries are a convenient sufficient proof, not a necessary condition. For disconnected same-color boundaries, check EVERY boundary group's remaining liberties when the opponent fills either eye. Here both retained the other eye; in game 9 A1 did not.
6. Never fill one of the upper shared eyes merely to connect J9. Both empty points are essential.
7. The corner rescue relied on an ignored atari. Preserve eye space earlier and keep opening/correction candidates hypothetical.

All decisions and tactical variations were manual. Code only parsed returned current boards, inventoried present groups/liberties and empty regions, recorded responses, converted moves to SGF and counted current final area. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

# Game 12: White vs 20k — B+12

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 56–57. There were 57 moves: 55 stone moves and two passes.
Final captures: Black 9, White 0. No ko, invalid move, resignation or dead-stone removal occurred.

The two wins in games 10–11 were followed by this loss. At 20k the series now has two wins and six losses. Stay at 20k: repeatable strength is not established, and the tactical/strategic failures recur despite current-board inventories.

## Records and verified score

- game-012.sgf contains all 57 moves.
- game-012-log.json contains selection, all 28 play responses, every returned board, current-board group/liberty and empty-region inventories, in-game counting notes, full move list and final area.
- Official result: Black wins by 12 points.
- Independent final-board count: Black 28 stones + 22 territory = 50; White 18 stones + 13 territory = 31. White plus komi = 38. All 81 points assigned; no neutral area.
- White area by rows 1 through 9: 0, 2, 3, 3, 4, 3, 5, 6, 5 = 31.
- White territory: A3/A4/A5/A6/A7/A8/A9, B4/B5/B6/B7, C9, D8.
- Black territory: E1/E2/E3/E4/F2/F3/G4; G1/H1/H2/H3/J1/J2/J3/J4; F6; H5/H6/H7; H9/J8/J9.
- Captured White stones: E1/E2/E3/E4/F2/F3 at move 27, then H5/H6/H7 at move 49.

## Early count: a geometric outline was not a base

Opening:
1 B G7, 2 W C3, 3 B G3, 4 W C7,
5 B F5, 6 W E3, 7 B E5, 8 W E7,
9 B E6, 10 W D5, 11 B F7, 12 W D7,
13 B D6, 14 W C6, 15 B D4, 16 W C5,
17 B D3, 18 W E4, 19 B D2.

Before move 10, the explicitly unsecured outline was columns A–D (36 points) plus E1/E2/E3/E7/E8/E9 (six): 42 potential points, zero secure territory. This count was early, but the plan failed to preserve its boundaries. Black D6 and D4/D3/D2 occupied points inside that outline and separated E3 from C3. The lower E-region was not a living base.

D7 joined C7 to the two-liberty E7 stone. C6 connected to the upper group; after Black D4 put D5 in atari with only C5, White C5 immediately joined D5 to C6. These repairs worked locally. They did not save the separate E3 group.

Reconsider the position before 18 W E4 and especially before 20 W F3: the left chain and the E3 stones are separate, and Black's D-line blocks access between them. Earlier C4 connection or a different center/right extension is a hypothesis to examine, not an established saving move. The game does not prove the initial C3/C7/E3/E7 opening loses, nor any specific replacement wins.

## Lower loss: extending two liberties into a forced capture

20 W F3, 21 B F4,
22 W F2, 23 B G2,
24 W E2, 25 B F1,
26 W E1, 27 B D1 captured six.

Current-board inventories:
- After move 19, E3/E4 had E2/F3/F4.
- After move 21, E3/E4/F3 had only E2/F2.
- After move 23, E3/E4/F2/F3 had only E2/F1.
- After move 25, E2/E3/E4/F2/F3 had only E1.
- W E1 was legal but left all six stones with only D1.
- B D1 joined Black D2 and captured all six, reopening E1/E2/E3/E4/F2/F3 as liberties for adjacent Black groups.

There was no eye, capture to open a useful liberty, or connection to the left group in the played continuation. The inventory was read every contact turn, yet its shrinking two-liberty corridor was treated as development. That is the core failure. The danger needed action before Black F4/G2/F1 closed successive boundaries, not merely another legal extension after atari.

Do not label E2 instead of F2 at move 22 a verified rescue: changing that move alone has not been shown to supply two eyes or a surviving connection. Nor does this game's loss invalidate game 10's F3/F2 sequence: the exact Black replies and open liberties differ. In game 10, captures supplied eyes; here Black defended and captured White.

## Top connection preserved stones but could not recover the deficit

28 W C4, 29 B C2,
30 W F8, 31 B G8,
32 W E8, 33 B F9,
34 W E9, 35 B G9.

C4 joined C3 to the left/upper chain. F8 had E8/F9 after Black G8; E8 promptly joined it to E7. E9 put F9 in atari, and Black G9 connected F9 to G8. No Black stone was captured.

After move 35, a coarse outline was only 33: columns A–C excluding C2/C1 (25), plus D5/D7/D8/D9 (four), E7/E8/E9 (three), F8 (one). The bottom boundary still was not settled. With all points assigned, White needs at least 38 area to win with 7 komi; 37 draws. Saving the left framework alone would not win.

## Right invasion: three edge liberties still did not make eyes

36 W H5, 37 B H4,
38 W H6, 39 B G6,
40 W H7, 41 B H8,
42 W C8, 43 B G5,
44 W D9, 45 B J7,
46 W B8, 47 B J6,
48 W B9, 49 B J5 captured three.

H5 was an attempted new base, but it began without a demonstrated two-eye or escape plan. H6/H7 grew the same narrow edge strip. Black H4 and H8 owned its lower and upper outside boundaries.

After move 41, H5/H6/H7 had G5/J5/J6/J7. Black G5 then connected the center and upper Black chains and left White only J5/J6/J7. These were a connected three-point edge space with unsecured J4/J8 boundaries, not two eyes. Black J7 and J6 reduced the group to J5, then J5 captured it.

After move 47, W J5 would be legal, but the four-stone group would have only J4. B J4 joins H4 and captures four. This is not ko. White instead abandoned the right stones and secured unconditional life on the left. Abandoning them did not make the initial invasion sound; do not reuse H5/H6/H7 as a living pattern.

The potential deficit should be contested while viable bases remain available. A late area-driven invasion still needs a life plan; the need for points does not supply missing eye boundaries.

## Surviving group's exact life and settled lower boundary

42 W C8 connected to C7.
44 W D9 connected through E9/E8.
46 W B8 connected to C8.
48 W B9 connected to B8.

The main group then had two independent true eyes:
- D8: bounded by C8/D7/E8/D9.
- C9: bounded by B9/C8/D9.
All boundary stones belong to the connected White group. D9 connected through E9, not diagonally through C8 or D7. Leave C9/D8 empty.

50 W B2, 51 B B1,
52 W B3, 53 B A1,
54 W A2, 55 B C1,
56 W pass, 57 B pass.

B3 immediately joined isolated B2 to C3. A2 joined B2 and denied a further left undercut; Black C1 connected A1/B1 to its D-line. White's final 18 stones all belonged to the living main group.

The independent final count was made before passing and matched B+12. No dead stones were removed by scoring.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k. Two wins followed by this loss do not establish consistency.
2. Use the liberty inventory to reject a closed development route. F3/F2/E2/E1 added stones but no eyes or escape; E1 was a legal one-liberty extension that lost six.
3. When Black separates the planned bases, revise the area outline immediately and identify an actual connection or alternate base before the remaining route closes.
4. An invasion for needed points still needs secured eye boundaries. H5/H6/H7 plus J5/J6/J7 failed after H4/H8 undercuts and G5 closure.
5. Preserve the local successes: D7/C5/C4/E8/B3 repaired real orthogonal connections, and C8/D9/B8/B9 established connected C9/D8 eye boundaries. These preserved the main group, but its 31 area was too small.

All decisions and tactical variations were manual. Code only parsed returned boards, inventoried current groups/liberties and empty regions, recorded responses, counted current area, and converted the move record to SGF. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

# Game 10: White vs 20k — W+10

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 63–64. There were 64 moves: 61 stone moves and three passes (61, 63, 64).
Final captures: Black 0, White 4. No ko, invalid move, resignation or dead-stone removal occurred.

This is the first win in the series, following five losses at 20k. It establishes one successful game at 20k, not consistent strength or an optimal opening. Retain 20k until wins and living groups are repeatable, including as Black.

## Records and verified score
- game-010.sgf contains all 64 moves.
- game-010-log.json contains opponent selection, all 32 play responses, every returned board, current-board group/liberty inventories, complete moves and independent area count.
- Official result: White wins by 10 points.
- Independent final-board count: Black 26 stones + 13 territory = 39; White 31 stones + 11 territory = 42. White plus komi = 49. All 81 points are assigned; no neutral points.
- White's lower group: 14 stones plus E1/D2/D3 = 17 area.
- White's upper group: 17 stones plus A9/C8/D9/E9/F9/G9/H9/J9 = 25 area.
- Upper area by rows: all nine points in row 9, all nine in row 8, B7/C7/D7/E7/G7 (five), and C6/D6 (two): 25.
- Black territory: A5 and H1/J1/H2/J2/H3/J3/H4/J4/G5/H5/J5/J6.
- Black captured no White stones. The four captured Black stones were E1 at move 24 and C2/D2/D3 at move 26.

## Lower fight: cut, pressure the shared escape, then secure the eyes
Opening:
1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B D3, 4 W C4, 5 B C5,
6 W D4, 7 B D5, 8 W E3, 9 B D2,
10 W E4, 11 B F4, 12 W F3, 13 B G4.

E3 put D3 in atari, and Black D2 extended downward. E4 joined E3 to C3/C4/D4; F3 extended into still-open lower-right space. Unlike the late E4 extension in game 8, this extension had more than one temporary destination.

14 W C7 established an upper foothold while the lower group still had options.
15 B B4, 16 W B3, 17 B C2, 18 W B2,
19 B B1, 20 W E2, 21 B E1.

B3/B2 answered the left-side pressure, but B1 undercut the first-line boundary. The group was not yet alive. After move 21, Black C2/D2/D3 had only C1/D1; Black E1 had D1/F1.

22 W F1 reduced E1 to D1. Black ignored this atari with 23 B A4.
24 W D1 captured E1 and put C2/D2/D3 in atari at C1.
Black ignored that atari with 25 B A3.
26 W C1 captured C2/D2/D3.
27 B A2 kept Black B1 in atari at A1 while connecting the left-edge Black stones.

F1 before D1 mattered. In the actual move-21 position, immediate W D1 would be a self-atari at C1; B C1 captures that stone and opens D1 for the Black group. After F1, W D1 instead captures E1, opening E1 as a second liberty for the new White stone.

Black's ignored ataris were concrete mistakes. The opening is not proven to force the played captures. A short manual alternative after W F1 is B D1 connecting E1 to C2/D2/D3; that joined five-stone Black group would have only C1, where White can capture it. This limited reading is not a proof of every alternative or a forced win.

The capture at C1 did not itself prove life. White C1/D1 and F1 were still separate from the main group, and the empty C2/D2/D3 region was connected.
28 W F2 connected F1 to E2/F3.
29 B B5, 30 W C2 connected C1/D1 through B2/C3 and closed the left boundary of D2/D3.

After move 30 the lower group had two independent secured eye spaces:
- E1: bounded by White D1/E2/F1, all connected.
- D2/D3: bounded by White D1/C2/E2/C3/E3/D4, all connected.
This life proof held when Black G3/G2/G1 closed the remaining outside liberties. The final lower group had exactly E1/D2/D3 as liberties and was alive.

White did not chase the atari Black B1 by W A1 after move 27. That would capture B1 but leave the new isolated A1 stone with only B1, introducing a simple-ko dependency. F2/C2 secured unconditional eyes elsewhere instead.

## Upper development: make the second base large enough and repair each connection
31 B G3, 32 W E7, 33 B G2, 34 W G7, 35 B G1.
The lower group stayed alive but shrank to 17 area. The earlier C7 foothold allowed White to develop the open upper side, rather than attempting another late lower-right invasion.

36 W C6, 37 B F5, 38 W D6, 39 B B6,
40 W B7, 41 B A7, 42 W A8, 43 B A6,
44 W B8, 45 B E6, 46 W D7.

B8 immediately joined A8 to B7. A8 had only B8/A9 after Black A6; leaving it disconnected would have allowed further pressure. D7 then joined the left upper chain to E7.

47 B F7 cut between E7 and G7, with only F6/F8.
48 W F8 put it in atari; 49 B F6 connected it to Black's main group.
50 W E8 connected F8 to the left upper chain.
51 B G6 left White G7 only H7/G8.
52 W G8 joined G7 to F8 before 53 B H7 removed H7.
54 W H8, 55 B H6, 56 W J8 closed the upper-right boundary.
57 B A1 connected Black B1 to the main group.
58 W D8, 59 B J7.

The choice of F8 rather than F6 at move 48 avoided a counter-atari trap: W F6 would have only G6, and B G6 could capture it, reopening F6 for Black F7. The actual F8 had E8/G8/F9 and supplied a viable connection.

## Settle the eyes before accepting the winning count
60 W B9, 61 B pass, 62 W C9, 63 B pass, 64 W pass.

B9 first connected to B8 and made a true eye at A9, bounded by A8/B9.
C9 then connected through B9 and made a second true eye at C8, bounded by B8/C7/D8/C9.
All boundaries belong to the connected upper group. D9–J9 remained a third, larger eye space.

C9 would not have connected directly to B8 or D8: those are diagonal neighbors. The actual B9–C9 sequence supplied the stone connection needed for the life proof.

The formal row/region count came late, around moves 52–63: 17 lower plus 25 upper = 42, enough to beat Black's 39 with komi. Early area estimates were provisional and were not recorded as a detailed secure/potential count around moves 10–16. Improve that timing next game; this win does not erase the counting weakness.

## Carry forward
1. Keep 20k for repeatability, especially as Black. One win does not establish consistent strength.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
13. An invasion can gain connected stones without gaining a base. Game 3's C8/D8/D7/C7/B7/D9 ended with only B8 and C9 as liberties. White A8/A7 and E9 denied eye boundaries. The later upper-right entry also failed; neither upper group was saved.
14. An extension must actually reach open space. In game 4, F4/F5/F6/E6 grew a connected chain without eyes. After Black E7, its remaining liberties were G1, G5, J1, J2, J3; the central escape was closed. The inventory ran every move, but did not prevent this strategic failure. Re-evaluate before the final route narrows to one point.
15. Preserving one corner boundary does not establish two eyes. Game 4's H1 prevented game 2's undercut, but Black H4 restricted the upper base. J3/J4/J5 added occupied edge stones, not eyes. At the end the thirteen-stone White group had only J1/J2: one two-point eye space. Black J2, White J1 captures one stone, Black J2 captures fourteen; this is not ko.
16. A threat may be answered by capturing its new stone. Game 4's G7 threatened Black G5/G6/H4/H5 but had only G8. Black G8 captured it and reopened G7 for three adjacent Black groups. Do not count such a threat as forcing.
17. Count playable escape points, not just raw liberties. In game 5, the top D8/D9/E8/E9 block had only D7, but Black D7 was suicide: White C7, D6 and E7 surrounded it and none would be captured. After White C8 at move 32, D9/E9 added stones without creating eyes or escape. The E8/F8/D8/C8/D9/C9/E9/F9 continuation failed.
18. A surviving framework can still be too small. Game 5's lower group scored 38 area against White's 43 plus komi. At that split, shifting six points from White to Black only draws; seven wins. Contest additional space before D6/F6 and the upper boundary close, rather than relying on a late first-line invasion.
19. Two shared liberties do not prove seki. In game 6 after move 19, White's eight-stone lower-left group and Black A2/B2 both had only A1/A3. Black A3, White A1 captured three, but Black A2 then occupied the vital point of A2/A3/B2. White A3 allows Black B2 to capture ten; White B2 allows Black A3 to capture ten. White instead played elsewhere and Black A3/B2 captured nine. The earlier claim of seki was wrong. Read beyond the first capture to the opponent's next turn.
20. A capture into a three-point eye space needs the dividing point before it supplies two eyes. In game 6, White A2 after capturing A2/A3/B2 would divide A3 and B2, but Black moved first and killed. By contrast, the upper group already had true eyes B9 (A9/B8/C9 boundaries) and E9 (D9/E8/F9 boundaries) before capturing H8/H9; all boundaries were connected White.
21. Reassess a second eye's boundary immediately after an undercut. Game 6 preserved J1 with H1/J2, but G1 required a surviving White F1 boundary. Black F2/F1/E1 connected to D1–D4, so G1 was not an eye. E4/F4/G4 led into a closed strip; Black G1/E4/F4/G4 left the eight-stone White group only J1, and Black J1 captured it. H1 alone again did not establish life.
22. Check where an atari extension ends before making the contact move. Game 6's B6 was left with only A6 by Black B7; White A6 would leave two stones with only A7, allowing Black A7 to capture both. White B8 secured the upper wall but Black A6 captured B6.

White H9 could capture two and open F9/G9 for the invaders. Actual White J9 at move 52 captured F9/G9/H9 and reopened F9/G9/H9. Black's attempted chase did not force a capture.

Losing seven top points left 31. The main group did live: G6 (F6/G5/G7/H6 boundaries) and J6 (H6/J5/J7 boundaries) were independent true eyes after H7 connected all boundaries.

Then Black G1, White F1, Black H1, White J1 would capture three. Black abandoned G2 instead; White G1 captured it. Do not treat the G2 entry as a proven living pattern.

# Game 13: Black vs 20k — B+6

Played 2026-10-05. 9x9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
Completed by consecutive passes at moves 88–89: 89 moves, 85 stone moves and four passes (84, 86, 88, 89).
Final captures: Black 15, White 4. One ko arose at G9 after White move 46; no recapture was attempted. No invalid move, resignation or dead-stone removal occurred.

The 20k series now has three wins and six losses. This win preserved the main group but lost four invading stones and needed a late opponent error to recover enough area. Retain 20k; the opening and invasion are not established winning patterns.

D7 joined D6 to C7; C6 promptly joined C5 to that upper chain. D3 joined C3 to E3 before White could separate them. White F3 then cut between E3 and G3. The game does not prove any of these moves optimal.

The row count after move 36 was only about 37: rows 1/2 nine each, row 3 eight, row 4 A/B/E/F four, row 5 A/B/C three, rows 6/7 C/D two each. This remained potential, with unsettled boundaries.

## Turning capture: read the counter-atari through the opened liberty

57 B A4, 58 W A6.

White A5/A6/B6/B7 had exactly A7/B8. Its undercut had joined the isolated A5 stone to a group with inadequate escape liberties.

This local reading is not proof that the opening forces the eventual capture. White's earlier A5/A6 undercut created this opportunity.

The main outline after White A5 was about 40. Capturing those four stones and adding A7/B8 brought the actual outline to 46; A8 added one, yielding the eventual 47. Life plus this concrete area gain justified playing for a scored win.

## Carry forward

1. Retain 20k. Three wins and six losses do not establish consistency; this win still lost four stones and needed opponent errors for enough area.
2. An early minimum-area outline is a warning to act earlier. Do not let top-left reductions close the board and then replace a territory plan with another unsupported edge invasion.
3. Do not reuse H7/H8/G9/J9 as life. G9's one-liberty boundary made the apparent eye ko-dependent; connecting it left one two-point space.
4. Read counter-ataris through the first capture. B8 was in atari, but A7 captured White B7 and reopened B7, saving B8. This is the same capture-liberty principle that previously caused losses, now used correctly.
5. Connect captured-area stones promptly. B7 joined both new left stones to a group already alive with F3/H3; no new corner-eye gamble was required.
6. Count rows carefully. The late outline was 41, not the recorded 42; final 47 was independently verified. Do not let a won game hide a counting error.

All move choices and tactical variations were manual. Code only inspected returned current boards, inventoried present stones/groups/liberties/empty regions, kept records, converted moves to SGF, and counted final area. No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, or automated move selection/ranking/recommendation was used.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
7. Game 2 counted an insecure right-side base as territory. Black G2 followed by H1 undermined the corner; J4/J5 occupied remaining eye space. The final seven-stone White right group had only H4 and J2 as liberties and a concrete forced-capture route. Connected second-line stones do not guarantee a base.
8. Use permitted current-board group/liberty inspection during contact fights. Game 2 missed that Black D3 put White D4/E4 in atari with only C4 available; White played J8 instead. Scan ALL own groups before pursuing a distant plan.
9. Before invading, identify two prospective eyes or a concrete escape/connection. Game 2's late G8/H7/J8 invasion had no demonstrated life; trapping H9 would provide only one prospective eye.
10. Check the opponent's simplest connection. In game 2, White E4 did not separate the lower Black stones: Black F4 joined F3 and F5 and squeezed White's right group.
11. Three connected empty edge points are not already two eyes. In game 3, White J8 occupied the middle of J7/J8/J9. Black J7, White J5 left the seven-stone upper-right group with only J9. Black J9 would capture J8 but leave the entire eight-stone group with only J8; White J8 captures it all. This is not ko. Simply substituting J8 for J6 at move 61 was not verified to save it: J6 also needed boundary protection.
12. Check the hane's cut and the new stone's own liberties. Game 3's A5 was left in atari by White B5; A6 was suicide. White A6 later captured A5 and reopened A5 for the neighboring White edge group. Black A1 then had only B1, and White B1 captured it, reopening A1. Both planned edge squeezes ignored liberties opened by captures.
